screens.title: Containerization Security Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we'll build a practical mental model for securing containerized applications. Containers package code, runtime, and libraries into images that share the host operating system kernel. That efficiency gives us agility, but it also changes where and how we defend systems. You will learn how provenance and image scanning stop vulnerable or malicious layers from entering your pipeline, how runtime controls — like least privilege, dropped capabilities, resource limits, and network policies — reduce the blast radius when something goes wrong, and how secrets management prevents credential leakage. We'll ground these ideas with concrete practices: pinning image versions, signing images, integrating scanning into CI/CD, running processes as non-root, and using dedicated secret stores rather than baking credentials into images or environment variables. You will also see common misconfigurations that produce real risk, such as using the latest tag or exposing the Docker daemon. By the end of the chapter you should be able to make clear, defensible decisions about image sourcing, runtime hardening, monitoring, and secret injection. Consider as you listen: where could an attacker gain access in your current process, and which single change would reduce that risk the most?

Module 4 › Chapter 4.4 › Containerization Security Fundamentals
Containerization Security Fundamentals
Protect images, runtimes, and secrets across the container lifecycle.
In this lesson

Learn to verify and scan images, run containers with least privilege, segment networks, and inject secrets securely at runtime. These practices reduce attack surface and make incidents containable.

Containers share a kernel. A single escalated container can affect the host and other containers. Proper image hygiene and runtime controls protect your infrastructure and data.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Implementation Milestones
screens.narratorSegment: Now we translate learning objectives into measurable actions. For understanding container fundamentals, inspect an image manifest and list its layers and packages so you can point to where runtime components come from. screens.title: What containers are and how they change threat models
screens.narratorSegment: Begin with a clear definition. A container image is a lightweight, standalone package that contains application code, runtime, libraries, and settings needed to run an application. Containers themselves are runtime instances of those images, produced by an engine such as Docker, and they use namespaces and cgroups for isolation while sharing the host kernel. This shared kernel model is the pivotal difference from virtual machines: VMs virtualize hardware and include their own kernels; containers rely on the host kernel. That matters because a kernel vulnerability or a malicious container can impact other containers or the host. A concrete example: if a web container is run as root and an exploit allows escalation, that container could attempt to access other containers or modify host files. A common misconception is believing that container isolation is equivalent to VM isolation; it is not. Containers provide strong process and filesystem separation but not a separate kernel. Key practical implications are to keep the host kernel patched, minimize container privileges, and use namespaces effectively. Takeaway: treat the host kernel as part of your attack surface and design controls assuming potential lateral movement.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Containers share the host kernel; this increases efficiency but means kernel-level vulnerabilities and privileged containers can compromise the host or peers.

content.html:
Core Concept What containers are
Container & Image Definition

A container image bundles code, runtime, libraries, and configuration into a repeatable unit. A container is the running instance that uses namespaces and cgroups to isolate processes and resources, while sharing the host kernel.

Analogy
Think of an image as a sealed appliance and the container as the appliance running in your kitchen: many appliances share the same power grid (kernel).
Misconception
Containers are not full VMs. Kernel-level issues can affect all containers on a host.
Practical implications
  • Keep host kernel and container runtime patched; a host compromise affects all containers.
  • Limit privileges inside containers to reduce potential impact of an exploit.
  • Use user namespaces to map container root to an unprivileged host user when possible.
Key Takeaway
Treat the shared kernel as part of the attack surface and design defenses accordingly.

screens.title: Container Images and Registries
screens.narratorSegment: Container images are built from base layers and often pulled from public or private registries. Provenance means you can trace where every layer came from and whether it has been approved. A concrete example: a developer pulls an unofficial base image that includes outdated libraries. If that image contains a known vulnerable package, every container built from it inherits the vulnerability. Image signing and digests provide integrity and immutability: pin to a digest to ensure the exact layers are used, and require a signature to verify the image author. Image scanning finds CVEs in layers and can also detect malware or misconfigurations. A common misuse is relying on the latest tag; this creates unpredictability because the underlying image can change without notice. Another risk is storing images in public registries without access controls. Mitigations include using trusted registries, pinning by digest, signing images, and scanning every image before it enters your pipeline. Finally, remember that scanning is a point-in-time check; incorporate scanning into CI so new vulnerabilities in dependencies are caught before deployment. Container Images and Registries means verify provenance with digests and signatures, avoid 'latest', and scan images before they enter the pipeline to reduce supply-chain risk.. In practical terms, provenance, signing, and the risks of untrusted images. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition Images & Registries
Provenance and Integrity

Use image digests to pin an exact image and digital signatures to validate the publisher. Provenance shows who produced each layer and when.

Best practice
Pin images to a digest and require signed images for production deployments.
Common mistake
Using the latest tag leads to unreviewed changes and unpredictable vulnerabilities.
Registry Risks
  • Public registries can host malicious or outdated images.
  • Access controls and immutability policies reduce unauthorized pushes.
  • Automated scanning on push or pull helps detect vulnerabilities early.
Example
Integrate a scanner to block images that exceed a CVE severity threshold from being promoted to production.

screens.title: Image scanning in CI/CD
screens.narratorSegment: Automated image scanning belongs in the CI/CD pipeline so vulnerabilities are caught before an image reaches production. A typical flow builds an image, pushes it to a staging registry, runs a scanner that reports CVEs and misconfigurations, and gates promotion based on a policy. For example, integrate a scanner that fails the build if high or critical CVEs are present, or that creates tickets for moderate issues. A concrete scenario: a pipeline builds an application image and the scanner flags a high-severity CVE in a system library. The pipeline fails, and the developer receives the report to update the dependency or use a patched base image. A common misconception is treating scanning as a one-time job; vulnerability databases update and new CVEs appear. Therefore, incorporate scheduled rescans for images in registries and alerts for new critical findings. In practice, choose a scanner that produces machine-readable output for automated gating and supports your registry. The core practice is to shift image scanning left and ensure the pipeline enforces the organization’s vulnerability policy consistently. Image scanning in CI/CD means shift scanning into ci: fail builds or block promotions when images exceed your vulnerability threshold and schedule rescans for persisted images.. In practical terms, automating vulnerability detection before deployment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Process Image Scanning in CI/CD
Pipeline Flow
  1. Build image and tag with immutable digest.
  2. Push to staging registry.
  3. Run vulnerability scanner and collect machine-readable report.
  4. Enforce a policy: fail or block promotion if severity threshold is exceeded.
Rescan persisted images periodically and alert when new critical CVEs appear for images in use.
Example scanner output

  "image":"myapp@sha256:abc123",

screens.title: Principle of Least Privilege for containers
screens.narratorSegment: The Principle of Least Privilege means granting only the permissions necessary for a container to perform its function. Practically, that starts with avoiding running processes as root inside the container. Use the USER instruction in a Dockerfile or container runtime settings to run as a non-root user. Next, drop unnecessary Linux capabilities such as CAP_NET_ADMIN or CAP_SYS_ADMIN; most application containers do not need them. User namespaces can map container root to an unprivileged host user, reducing the impact if a container process is compromised. A concrete example: a web server container does not need CAP_NET_RAW or SYS_ADMIN to serve HTTP; drop those capabilities explicitly. Misconceptions include thinking capabilities are all-or-nothing; in fact, Linux capabilities are modular and can be removed with fine granularity. Finally, note that running as non-root alone is not a silver bullet — it should be combined with read-only root filesystems, immutable images, and network controls. Ask yourself: which privileges does this service actually need, and which can we remove safely? Principle of Least Privilege for containers means run containers as non-root, drop unnecessary capabilities, and consider user namespace mapping to limit host exposure.. In practical terms, non-root users, capabilities, and user namespaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Core Practice Least Privilege
Practical controls
  • Use USER in Dockerfile to avoid root processes.
  • Drop capabilities with --cap-drop and add only if needed.
  • Use read-only root filesystems where possible.
Add an audit rule that flags any deployment granting SYS_ADMIN or privileged mode so reviewers can catch risky changes.
Example
A simple Dockerfile change from running as root to creating and switching to a non-root user reduces the ability of an attacker to modify host files if they break out.
Key Takeaway
Least privilege reduces exploit impact; combine it with other runtime controls for layered defense.

screens.title: Immutable infrastructure and build practices
screens.narratorSegment: Immutable infrastructure means treating containers and images as immutable artifacts: if you need to change configuration or code, you build a new image and redeploy rather than modifying a running container. This approach reduces configuration drift, simplifies auditing, and makes rollbacks reliable. A typical workflow builds an image from source and a deterministic base, runs tests, signs the image, and pushes a uniquely tagged digest to the registry. If a configuration change is required, update the source, rebuild, and create a new image rather than changing a live container. A concrete example: rotating application configuration or secrets should be done by creating a new image or by injecting updated secrets at runtime using a secret store. A misconception is thinking immutability prevents all operational fixes; it simply changes the pattern for fixes: do them via new builds or controlled runtime injection mechanisms. Immutable practices pair well with automation, CI/CD gating, and declarative deployment descriptors so you can reproduce any environment exactly from artifacts and configuration. Immutable infrastructure and build practices means treat containers as immutable artifacts: rebuild and redeploy instead of modifying running containers to reduce drift and simplify audits.. In practical terms, build once, redeploy rather than patching running containers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow Immutable Infrastructure
Build once, deploy many
  1. Build deterministic image from source and pinned base.
  2. Run tests and sign the image.
  3. Push artifact tagged by digest to registry.
  4. Deploy using pinned digest and declarative manifests.
Operational benefits
  • Simplifies audits because deployed images are reproducible.
  • Reduces drift by avoiding ad-hoc changes on running containers.
  • Makes rollbacks straightforward by switching to a previous digest.
Key Takeaway
Immutable images plus CI/CD produce auditable, repeatable deployments that are easier to secure.

screens.title: Resource limits and denying DoS by rogue containers
screens.narratorSegment: Resource limits are a practical control to prevent a single container from exhausting host C P U or memory and causing a denial-of-service for other services. Use container runtime or orchestration descriptors to set resource requests and limits. Requests inform the scheduler what the container needs; limits cap the maximum usage. For example, a runaway process that consumes all memory can crash the host or trigger OOM kills that destabilize services. By setting a memory limit of 256 megabytes for a small service, you reduce the chance that it monopolizes resources. A common misconception is that limits eliminate DoS risk entirely; they reduce the blast radius but do not stop application-level abuse such as excessive requests. Resource limits work best combined with rate limiting, autoscaling, and monitoring. Also profile normal resource usage so limits are realistic and do not trigger unnecessary restarts. Key takeaway: resource limits are a straightforward way to make containerized deployments more robust and predictable under load or compromise. Resource limits and denying DoS by rogue containers means set realistic cpu and memory requests and limits to prevent individual containers from impacting the entire host or cluster.. In practical terms, cpu, memory, and quotas to contain resource consumption. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition Resource Limits
Why limits matter

Limits prevent a single container from consuming all host resources. They are part of graceful degradation and defense-in-depth for availability.

Practical rule
Profile expected usage and set requests close to normal use and limits at a safe cap to allow for spikes without host exhaustion.
Combined defenses
  • Resource limits + autoscaling handle load surges gracefully.
  • Rate limiting prevents application-level overload.
  • Monitoring and alerts let you detect resource anomalies quickly.

screens.title: Network segmentation with Kubernetes Network Policies
screens.narratorSegment: Network segmentation reduces the ability of a compromised container to reach sensitive services. In Kubernetes, network policies declare which pods can talk to which endpoints. A typical policy allows only the application tier to speak to the database tier and blocks all other traffic. For example, create a network policy that selects database pods and permits ingress only from pods labeled as the frontend application on the database port. A common error is relying on namespace separation alone; network policies provide finer-grained controls based on labels and ports. Another misconception is that policies are global by default; without a policy many network plugins allow broad communication. Operationally, adopt a default-deny posture and then open minimal rules needed for operation. Finally, test policies in a staging environment and add monitoring to verify expected flows. The result is reduced lateral movement and clearer attack surface boundaries between application components. content.html:
Process Flow Kubernetes Network Policy
Default-deny strategy

Start with no allowed ingress and egress, then add explicit policies that permit necessary communication by label and port.

Testing policies in staging ensures legitimate flows remain functional before enforcement in production.
Example policy
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: db-allow-from-frontend
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: database
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: frontend
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 5432
This policy permits only pods labeled front-end to connect to the database on the specified port.

Architecture Runtime Monitoring
What to monitor
  • Unexpected process execution inside containers.

Operational pattern
Feed runtime events to an incident response pipeline, create alert playbooks, and tune detectors to reduce noise. Use containment actions such as isolating the pod or scaling down the deployment when confirmed anomalies occur.

Monitoring replaces patching — it does not. Use both patching/scanning and runtime detection together.

screens.title: Secrets management for containers
screens.narratorSegment: Secrets such as A P I keys, database credentials, or encryption keys must not be baked into images or stored in plaintext environment variables checked into source control. Use a dedicated secrets manager that provides secure storage, controlled access, and rotation. In Kubernetes, Kubernetes Secrets or an external solution like Vault or a cloud key store can inject secrets at runtime as files or ephemeral environment variables, without baking them into the image. A practical approach: grant the runtime service account access to a secret only at pod start, and rotate the secret regularly while using an automated injection mechanism. A common misconception is that environment variables are secure; they can be exposed in logs or by misconfigured process listings. Also avoid committing configuration files with embedded secrets to your repository. Conceptually, treat secrets as runtime-only assets accessible through authenticated, auditable channels. Ask yourself: who can read this secret, how is it rotated, and how is access audited? content.html:
Core Practice Secrets Management
Principles
  • Never bake secrets into images or commit them to source control.
  • Use an authenticated secrets store with access controls and rotation.
  • Inject secrets at runtime and mount them as files when possible.
Conceptual example
# Concept: inject secret at pod start
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: app
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: myapp@sha256:...
    env:
    - name: DB_PASSWORD
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef:
          name: db-secret
          key: password
Use a secret backend that supports rotation and auditing rather than static values in the image.

screens.title: Common container security mistakes and quick defenses
screens.narratorSegment: Security issues often arise from simple, repeatable mistakes. One frequent mistake is using the latest image tag; it makes deployments unpredictable and can silently introduce new vulnerabilities. Defense: pin images to digests and review changes before promotion. Another is running privileged containers or granting broad capabilities which breaks isolation. Defense: drop capabilities and use non-privileged users. Exposing the Docker daemon or container runtime A P I without authentication is a critical risk because it grants control over the host. Defense: lock down the daemon with TLS and restrict access. Skipping vulnerability scanning is also common; the defense is to automate scanning in CI and set promotion policies. Finally, ignoring host OS security undermines container-level controls — keep the kernel and runtime patched and monitored. The practical pattern is defense-in-depth: apply image hygiene, runtime hardening, network rules, secrets management, and monitoring together so that when one control fails, others still limit impact. Using latest tag
Risk: unpredictable changes and hidden vulnerabilities. Defense: pin to digest and require review.
Privileged containers
Risk: breaks isolation and can lead to host compromise. Defense: avoid privileged mode and drop unnecessary capabilities.

Risk: remote control of host. Defense: secure the API with TLS and strict access control.

Risk: unknown CVEs reach production. Defense: integrate scanners into CI and schedule rescans.

Risk: leaked credentials. Defense: use secret stores and inject at runtime.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll build a practical mental model for securing containerized applications. Containers package code, runtime, and libraries into images that share the host operating system kernel. That efficiency gives us agility, but it also changes where and how we defend systems. You will learn how provenance and image scanning stop vulnerable or malicious layers from entering your pipeline, how runtime controls — like least privilege, dropped capabilities, resource limits, and network policies — reduce the blast radius when something goes wrong, and how secrets management prevents credential leakage. We'll ground these ideas with concrete practices: pinning image versions, signing images, integrating scanning into CI/CD, running processes as non-root, and using dedicated secret stores rather than baking credentials into images or environment variables. You will also see common misconfigurations that produce real risk, such as using the latest tag or exposing the Docker daemon. By the end of the chapter you should be able to make clear, defensible decisions about image sourcing, runtime hardening, monitoring, and secret injection. Consider as you listen: where could an attacker gain access in your current process, and which single change would reduce that risk the most?

These learning objectives focus your study and map to practical outcomes you can demonstrate. First, understand containerization fundamentals: be able to explain what a container image contains and why containers share the host kernel. That foundation helps you reason about attack surface. Second, identify and mitigate image and registry risks: you will learn how to verify image provenance, pin versions, sign images, and run vulnerability scans. Third, implement secure runtime practices: apply least privilege, drop unnecessary Linux capabilities, set resource limits, and use network policies to segment traffic. Fourth, manage secrets and scanning: you will learn to avoid baking credentials into images, and to use secret stores and automated vulnerability scanning integrated into CI/CD. Each objective includes a short skill-check you can use in an audit or conversation with engineers. Practice these objectives as tasks: inspect an image manifest, add image scanning to a pipeline, and configure a pod to run as non-root. These tasks translate the concepts into repeatable controls you can verify in production.

Now we translate learning objectives into measurable actions. For understanding container fundamentals, inspect an image manifest and list its layers and packages so you can point to where runtime components come from. For image and registry risk mitigation, configure your pipeline to reject unsigned images or those failing a vulnerability threshold, and pin base images to specific digests. For runtime hardening, change container processes to run as a non-root user, explicitly drop NET_ADMIN or SYS_ADMIN capabilities the container does not need, and apply C P U and memory limits in deployment descriptors. For secrets and scanning, integrate a scanner into pre-merge checks and use a secret store that injects secrets at pod start instead of baking them into the image. Verification is simple: add automated checks in CI, audit a running pod for its user and capabilities, and validate secrets are not present in your container images. These implementation milestones help you prove to auditors and operators that the objectives are not theory but practiced controls.

Begin with a clear definition. A container image is a lightweight, standalone package that contains application code, runtime, libraries, and settings needed to run an application. Containers themselves are runtime instances of those images, produced by an engine such as Docker, and they use namespaces and cgroups for isolation while sharing the host kernel. This shared kernel model is the pivotal difference from virtual machines: VMs virtualize hardware and include their own kernels; containers rely on the host kernel. That matters because a kernel vulnerability or a malicious container can impact other containers or the host. A concrete example: if a web container is run as root and an exploit allows escalation, that container could attempt to access other containers or modify host files. A common misconception is believing that container isolation is equivalent to VM isolation; it is not. Containers provide strong process and filesystem separation but not a separate kernel. Key practical implications are to keep the host kernel patched, minimize container privileges, and use namespaces effectively. Takeaway: treat the host kernel as part of your attack surface and design controls assuming potential lateral movement.

Container images are built from base layers and often pulled from public or private registries. Provenance means you can trace where every layer came from and whether it has been approved. A concrete example: a developer pulls an unofficial base image that includes outdated libraries. If that image contains a known vulnerable package, every container built from it inherits the vulnerability. Image signing and digests provide integrity and immutability: pin to a digest to ensure the exact layers are used, and require a signature to verify the image author. Image scanning finds CVEs in layers and can also detect malware or misconfigurations. A common misuse is relying on the latest tag; this creates unpredictability because the underlying image can change without notice. Another risk is storing images in public registries without access controls. Mitigations include using trusted registries, pinning by digest, signing images, and scanning every image before it enters your pipeline. Finally, remember that scanning is a point-in-time check; incorporate scanning into CI so new vulnerabilities in dependencies are caught before deployment. Container Images and Registries means verify provenance with digests and signatures, avoid 'latest', and scan images before they enter the pipeline to reduce supply-chain risk.. In practical terms, provenance, signing, and the risks of untrusted images. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Automated image scanning belongs in the CI/CD pipeline so vulnerabilities are caught before an image reaches production. A typical flow builds an image, pushes it to a staging registry, runs a scanner that reports CVEs and misconfigurations, and gates promotion based on a policy. For example, integrate a scanner that fails the build if high or critical CVEs are present, or that creates tickets for moderate issues. A concrete scenario: a pipeline builds an application image and the scanner flags a high-severity CVE in a system library. The pipeline fails, and the developer receives the report to update the dependency or use a patched base image. A common misconception is treating scanning as a one-time job; vulnerability databases update and new CVEs appear. Therefore, incorporate scheduled rescans for images in registries and alerts for new critical findings. In practice, choose a scanner that produces machine-readable output for automated gating and supports your registry. The core practice is to shift image scanning left and ensure the pipeline enforces the organization’s vulnerability policy consistently. Image scanning in CI/CD means shift scanning into ci: fail builds or block promotions when images exceed your vulnerability threshold and schedule rescans for persisted images.. In practical terms, automating vulnerability detection before deployment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The Principle of Least Privilege means granting only the permissions necessary for a container to perform its function. Practically, that starts with avoiding running processes as root inside the container. Use the USER instruction in a Dockerfile or container runtime settings to run as a non-root user. Next, drop unnecessary Linux capabilities such as CAP_NET_ADMIN or CAP_SYS_ADMIN; most application containers do not need them. User namespaces can map container root to an unprivileged host user, reducing the impact if a container process is compromised. A concrete example: a web server container does not need CAP_NET_RAW or SYS_ADMIN to serve HTTP; drop those capabilities explicitly. Security issues often arise from simple, repeatable mistakes. One frequent mistake is using the latest image tag; it makes deployments unpredictable and can silently introduce new vulnerabilities. Defense: pin images to digests and review changes before promotion. Another is running privileged containers or granting broad capabilities which breaks isolation. Defense: drop capabilities and use non-privileged users. Exposing the Docker daemon or container runtime A P I without authentication is a critical risk because it grants control over the host. Defense: lock down the daemon with TLS and restrict access. Skipping vulnerability scanning is also common; the defense is to automate scanning in CI and set promotion policies. Finally, ignoring host OS security undermines container-level controls — keep the kernel and runtime patched and monitored. The practical pattern is defense-in-depth: apply image hygiene, runtime hardening, network rules, secrets management, and monitoring together so that when one control fails, others still limit impact. Let's summarize the core concepts to keep in mind. Containerization packages applications and dependencies into images that share the host kernel, so kernel security matters. Container images are immutable artifacts that should be pinned, signed, and scanned to prevent vulnerable or malicious layers from reaching production. Registries store and distribute images; restrict access and enable scanning at push or pull. Image scanning finds known CVEs and misconfigurations and should be integrated into CI/CD. Least privilege means running containers with the minimum permissions and dropping unnecessary Linux capabilities. Secrets management uses secure stores and runtime injection to avoid embedding credentials in images. Kubernetes Network Policies are declarative rules that control pod communication and should enforce a default-deny model. Runtime security monitoring detects anomalous behavior that scanning cannot, enabling rapid response. Keep these concise concepts in mind as a checklist when you design or audit containerized systems.

Finish with three short practical reminders you can use right away. First, always pin and sign images: immutable digests and signatures prevent accidental or malicious substitution. Second, enforce least privilege at runtime: non-root users, dropped capabilities, read-only filesystems, and resource limits make compromise harder to escalate. Third, avoid embedding secrets: use a dedicated secret manager that injects secrets at runtime and supports rotation and auditing. These three steps are not exhaustive, but they produce immediate risk reduction and are easy to start with in most environments.
